chapter: Cafe Society and the Zodiac Suite
title: Norman Granz, Milton Orent and the Philharmonic offer
summary: Norman Granz asked her to play with Jazz at the Philharmonic and got permission for the symphony. Milton Orent, a weird-sounding composer, taught her; they co-wrote 'In the Land of Oo-Bla-Dee' and she helped Miles with the tuba idea.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Then later Norman Granz came through with this new Jazz at the Philharmonic and he asked me if I'd play with them. I was very popular then, you know, drawing big crowds so I told him yes, if you will get permission for me to play with the New York Symphony, and I'll play for you for nothing. So he did. Mr. Ripp was the manager then. (movements) What I did was to arrange three of the Zodiac Suite. I had Brent Milton Aranda who was way out, way ahead of Coltrane or anybody. I don't know if you ever heard of him.

He played - not a very good musician but he was more or less a writer, composer, and he had studied all these weird sounds. Often when we had the jazz musicians up here like Sarah Vaughan and all of them, they couldn't stand to hear these chords and things that he was playing. They sounded like discords and whatnot. They'd leave. Milton taught me a great deal. That's the reason I kept up with the times and what was happening. During that period we both wrote "In the Land of Oo-Bla-Dee". He started it and I helped him a little with it.
When you say you helped a little bit - ?
I didn't do a heck of a lot but I did enough to get the name on. He'd always start things like, we set

Benny Goodman things. We were sitting in the car and he started whistling a tune. I said, "Gee, that would be good. I'm going upstairs and write it," you know. He always flushed me with ideas. There was never a lull; there was always something new happening. The first sound that Miles got with the tuba and all that - well, Miles was here and he said, "I'd like a tuba." Somebody said, "I'd like this instrument," and so forth and so on. Miles went out and he called back and said, "Thank you, Lou," and that's how he got his sound going. See, because we were really happy in creating and doing things and helping one another. Milton was really terrific. I have some arrangements and things here that he wrote when I was still out.
